title: numpy arrays
story:
An array is fast because it makes a promise: every element is the same type and the same width, laid out end to end in one contiguous block. Shape and strides describe it completely, the loop runs in compiled code, and a slice can be handed back as a view onto the same memory rather than a copy. That promise is the whole engine.

Collected data breaks the promise in three ways, and it is worth knowing which one you are hitting, because each has a different escape and only one of them is cheap. Text of varying length is the first: the type can be widened to the longest string present, which pads every shorter one, or the array can fall back to holding pointers to ordinary objects — at which point it is a list wearing an array's interface, and the contiguity that made it fast is gone. Mixed types in one column is the second, and it ends the same way. Holes are the third, and they are the interesting one.

There is no missing value inside an integer type. The not-a-number value is a floating point value — that is where it is defined and the only place it lives — so a column of integers with one absent entry cannot stay a column of integers. Assigning it directly raises. What happens in practice is quieter: the column is widened to double precision, the hole is filled with the floating point absence, and nothing complains.

That widening is lossy in a specific and unlucky place. A double carries a 53 bit significand, so it represents every integer exactly up to two to the fifty-third, which is 9007199254740992, and above that the spacing between representable values grows — at that boundary it is already 2. Identifiers are routinely larger. So a 64-bit identifier column that acquires one missing value becomes a column of doubles in which two adjacent identifiers can land on the same value and compare equal. Nothing raised, nothing was corrupted by any single operation, and two distinct customers are now one.

The escape is to stop letting the type be inferred. Declare it. If a column is an identifier, it is a label and not a quantity — nobody ever adds two of them — so it belongs in a string or in an explicitly nullable integer type that carries its missingness in a separate mask instead of encoding it in the value. The general habit for this whole track: the dtype of a column is a claim about the data, and claims should be written down rather than guessed at load time.

problem.name: Homogeneous typing
problem.shape: A fast container requires every element to share one type and one width, and the data you actually collected has holes, text and mixed types in it.
tell: the column types were never declared, only inferred at load
an identifier column is stored as a number
a column that should be whole numbers has a decimal point in it
a count of distinct entities is lower than it ought to be
problem.move: Declare the type of every column at the boundary instead of letting it be inferred. Hold identifiers as text, because they are labels rather than quantities. Where a genuinely numeric column can be absent, use a type that carries missingness in a separate mask rather than one that encodes it in the value.
problem.invariant: The container holds one type at one width. Any value that does not fit forces the whole column to a type that does, and the widening is chosen for representability rather than for fidelity.
problem.breaks: The promotion is lossy exactly where it is least visible. Widening preserves every value it can represent and silently rounds the ones it cannot, so the failure is not an error at the point of widening but an equality that becomes true later, in a join or a distinct count, far from the operation that caused it.

cost.time: nothing at load; the type declaration is written once
cost.space: a nullable integer type carries a mask alongside the values, which is roughly a bit per row, against a promotion to double which costs nothing extra in width and everything in fidelity
cost.beats: inferring types on read, which works until the first missing value and then changes the meaning of a column without changing its name

worked.problem: One missing value appeared in your identifier column, and now two different identifiers compare equal. Nothing raised an exception. What happened?
worked.reasoning:
Because the column stopped being integers, and the type it became cannot tell those two identifiers apart.

There is no absent value inside an integer type. The not-a-number marker is a floating point value; it exists in that type and nowhere else. So when one entry goes missing, the column cannot remain integers — assigning the absence directly raises an error, and the loader instead does the accommodating thing and widens the whole column to double precision.

Double precision has a 53 bit significand. Every integer up to two to the fifty-third is exactly representable, and two to the fifty-third is 9007199254740992. Past that point not every integer has its own representation: at the boundary the spacing is already 2, so consecutive integers start sharing. A 64-bit identifier is comfortably past it.

So two different identifiers, differing by one, now both round to the same double and compare equal. No single step did anything wrong. The widening was correct and necessary, the rounding was correct for the type, and the comparison honestly reported equality of the values it was given. The information was discarded between the two.

What makes it dangerous is where it surfaces: a join matches rows that should not have matched, a count of distinct entities comes out low, two customers merge. The loss is upstream of every one of those symptoms and invisible at each of them.

The fix is to refuse the premise. An identifier is a label, not a quantity — nobody sums two identifiers — so it should be held as a string, or in an explicitly nullable integer type that stores missingness in a separate mask rather than encoding it in the value. And the habit that prevents the whole class: declare the type of every column on load rather than letting it be inferred, because inference is a guess that gets re-made every time the data changes.

THE PROMISE

   -> shape + strides describe it completely

   nobody adds two identifiers.

problem.practice: Build a column of 64-bit identifiers above two to the fifty-third, check that they are distinct, then introduce a single missing value and check the type and the distinct count again. Then repeat it with the identifiers held as text and with a nullable integer type, and note which of the three still knows how many entities you have.

beats.broke: The array is fast because it promises that every element shares one type and one width in a contiguous block, and collected data breaks that promise three ways: varying-length text, mixed types, and holes.
beats.fix: Treat the type of a column as a declaration made deliberately rather than a guess made at load, and know which escape you are taking when the promise cannot be kept — widen the type, fall back to holding pointers, or carry missingness in a separate mask.
beats.cost: The widening is automatic, silent and lossy in one unlucky place: there is no absent value inside an integer type, so one hole promotes the column to double precision, and past two to the fifty-third that representation can no longer tell adjacent identifiers apart.

interview.q: One missing value appeared in your identifier column, and now two different identifiers compare equal. Nothing raised. What happened?
interview.trap: Looking for the operation that corrupted the data. No single step did anything wrong — the promotion was necessary, the rounding correct for the type, the comparison honest — and that is precisely why it is hard to find.
interview.answer:
Because the column is no longer integers, and the type it became cannot distinguish those two values.

An integer type has no representation for absence. The not-a-number marker is a floating point value and exists only there. So one missing entry makes the integer column impossible — assigning the absence directly raises — and the accommodating thing happens instead: the whole column is widened to double precision, quietly.

Double precision carries a 53 bit significand, which represents every integer exactly up to two to the fifty-third, or 9007199254740992. Above that the spacing grows; at the boundary it is already 2, so consecutive integers begin sharing a representation. A 64-bit identifier sits well past it, so two identifiers differing by one now round to the same double and compare equal.

Nothing in that chain is a bug. The promotion was necessary, the rounding is correct for the type, and the comparison faithfully reports what it was handed. The information was destroyed between the steps, and every symptom appears downstream of the destruction — a join matching rows it should not, a distinct count coming out low, two entities merging into one.

The fix is to reject the framing. An identifier is a label rather than a quantity; nobody adds two of them. Hold it as a string, or in an explicitly nullable integer type that carries missingness in a separate mask instead of encoding it in the value.

More generally, I would declare column types at load time rather than letting them be inferred, because inference is a guess that is quietly re-made every time the input changes — and this particular guess is re-made the first day a value goes missing.

blueprint:
WHAT THE ARRAY SELLS YOU

   uniformity  ->  speed
   one type, one width, one block

WHAT REAL DATA COSTS YOU

   text      -> widen-and-pad, or pointers
   mixed     -> pointers
   HOLES     -> promotion to float

THE PROMOTION, AND WHY IT BITES

   no not-a-number inside an integer type
      (it is a FLOAT. it lives nowhere else.)

   int64 + one hole  ->  float64

   float64: 53-bit significand
      exact up to  2^53 = 9007199254740992
      spacing at   2^53 = 2

      ...992 and ...993  ->  the SAME double

   64-bit ids live past that line.

SYMPTOMS, ALL DOWNSTREAM OF THE LOSS

   a join matches what should not have matched
   distinct-count comes out low
   two customers become one

   the loss is upstream of all three
   and invisible at each

THE RULE

   a dtype is a CLAIM about the data.
   write claims down. do not infer them.
   identifiers are labels -> strings or a
   nullable integer type with a mask.
takeaway: A column's type is a claim about the data, and leaving it to inference means the claim gets re-made every time the input changes — one missing value turns an identifier column into doubles, and past two to the fifty-third that type cannot tell two customers apart.
